Search and rescue: detection, coverage and the best use of effort

Source: vignettes/search-and-rescue.Rmd
search-and-rescue.Rmd

Search theory began with Koopman’s work for the U.S. Navy (1946) and is how search and rescue services plan a search: how likely a sensor is to see the object at a given distance, how much ground a search covers, how likely the object is to be in each area, and where a limited effort does the most good. Frost’s The Theory of Search: A Simplified Explanation (1996) explains it for search planners in four chapters of figures. This vignette walks those chapters and draws every one of the book’s 36 figures with srchfig(), which builds each from the package’s functions with the book’s parameters. srchfig() with no argument lists them and says how each is drawn: from the model, as a schematic, or as an approximation where the book’s plate cannot be recovered exactly.

table(srchfig()$how)
#> 
#> approximation         model     schematic 
#>             3            29             4

The functions behind the figures work on any inputs: ltrlrng() (lateral range curves), swpwdth() (sweep width), srchpod() and pswppod() (probability of detection), srchscs() (probability of success and the update after a search), datumpmap() (where the object may be), opteffort(), optcrcsrch() and optsqr() (the best use of effort). The book’s figures come first; Your own search then runs each function on numbers of your own.

Datums and probability maps

Figure 3-1. A point datum is a circular normal distribution of possible positions. The probability that the object is within R standard deviations of the datum is POC = 1 - exp(-R^2 / 2).

srchfig("3-1")

Figures 3-2, 3-3 and 3-5. The square circumscribed about a circle of radius R holds (2 Phi(R) - 1)^2 of the distribution: 47% for one standard deviation, 58% for the total probable error of position E = sqrt(2 ln 2) = 1.1774 standard deviations (the radius holding 50%), and 65% for the simplified method’s first search radius of 1.1 E.

srchfig("3-2")

srchfig("3-3")

srchfig("3-5")

Figure 3-4. A probability map lays a grid over the distribution. With cells 2E wide the centre holds 57.91%, a side cell 9.08% and a corner 1.42%.

srchfig("3-4")

Figures 3-6 and 3-7. The simplified method extended a point datum to a line by drawing circles at the two end points and boxing them in. The density this implies is drawn as a circular normal spread along the segment (datum = "line"), an approximation of the book’s plate.

srchfig("3-6")

srchfig("3-7")

Figures 3-8 to 3-10. A simpler line datum is normal across the line and uniform along it, with nothing beyond its ends (datum = "corridor"). A strip one standard deviation either side holds 68%, a strip of 2E holds 76.1%, and dividing strips into cells along the line gives the completed map of figure 3-10.

srchfig("3-8")

srchfig("3-9")

srchfig("3-10")

Figures 3-11 and 3-12. An area datum spreads the probability evenly: each of 20 equal cells holds 5%.

srchfig("3-11")

srchfig("3-12")

Figures 3-13 and 3-14. A generalized datum takes the planner’s own cell probabilities (datum = "general", wts =). The book’s surface is illustrative; here it is drawn from the cells of figure 3-14.

srchfig("3-13")

srchfig("3-14")

Lateral range curves and sweep width

Figure 4-1. A lateral range curve p(x) is the probability of detecting an object that passes at distance x from the track. The sweep width is its area, W = integral of p(x) dx; the dashed rectangles have the same area.

srchfig("4-1")

Figures 4-2 and 4-3. A definite range sensor sees everything within W / 2 of its track and nothing beyond: it sweeps a strip exactly W wide.

srchfig("4-2")

srchfig("4-3")

Figures 4-4 and 4-5. The M-Beta curve has height M over a width of W / M; with M = 0.5 and M = 0.25 the sweep width is unchanged.

srchfig("4-4")

srchfig("4-5")

Figures 4-6 and 4-7. Koopman’s inverse cube law takes the chance of a glimpse to be proportional to the solid angle of the wake, k h / r^3, which gives p(x) = 1 - exp(-W^2 / (4 pi x^2)). Its sweep width is W: the objects missed inside the sweep width (A) balance those seen outside it (B).

srchfig("4-6")

srchfig("4-7")

swpwdth(ltrlrng(seq(-500, 500, by = 0.01), W = 1))
#> [1] 0.9996817

Effort, coverage and probability of detection

Figure 5-1. Search effort is sweep width times track length, Z = W L, and coverage is effort over area, C = Z / A. A search whose path is random gives POD = 1 - exp(-C).

srchfig("5-1")

Figures 5-2 to 5-5. A parallel sweep at track spacing S has coverage C = W / S. With a definite range sensor the POD is min(C, 1): half the gap is seen at S = 2W, all of it at S = W.

srchfig("5-2")

srchfig("5-3")

srchfig("5-4")

srchfig("5-5")

Figures 5-6 and 5-7. M-Beta curves overlap once the tracks are closer than their width: POD = C below C = M and 1 - (1 - M)^(C / M) above it, 0.75 and 0.6836 at coverage 1 for M = 0.5 and M = 0.25, nearer the random search curve as M falls.

srchfig("5-6")

srchfig("5-7")

srchpod(c(0.5, 1, 2), "mbeta", m = 0.25)
#> ╭── Probability of detection ─────────────────────────────────────────╮
#> │   Model      M-Beta                                                 │
#> │   M          0.25                                                   │
#> │   Coverages  3                                                      │
#> │                                                                     │
#> │   coverage       pod                                                │
#> │   --------  --------                                                │
#> │    0.50000  0.437500                                                │
#> │    1.00000  0.683594                                                │
#> │    2.00000  0.899887                                                │
#> │                                                                     │
#> │   M-Beta model, M = 0.25                                            │
#> │   Coverage is effort over area (sweep width x track length / area); │
#> │   pod is the chance a search at that coverage finds the object.     │
#> ╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

Figure 5-8. The inverse cube parallel sweep gives POD = erf(sqrt(pi) C / 2), 0.7899 at coverage 1, between the definite range and random search curves. pswppod() computes the same sweep directly, for any curve.

srchfig("5-8")

pswppod(W = 1, S = 1)
#> [1] 0.7899086

Figure 5-9. Poorer conditions shrink the sweep width, and a cross-track navigation error of standard deviation sigma flattens the curve: the expected curve is the convolution phi(x) = integral of p(x - t) Z(t, sigma) dt, whose area is still W (ltrlrng(..., navsd = )). The plate is blank in the published file; it is drawn from the text.

srchfig("5-9")

Optimal search

Figures 6-1 and 6-2. With half the probability in a 3 by 3 square inside a 5 by 5 one and effort for half the area, the trial squares of the whole area, half of it and a third of it hold 100%, 60.94% and 46.30%; at coverage 1 the middle trial succeeds most often.

srchfig("6-1")

srchfig("6-2")

Figures 6-3 and 6-4. For a point datum, optsqr() finds the square that an effort, spread evenly, should cover: the search factor is its half side in units of E. An effort of 4 E^2 gives a factor of 1.02, coverage 0.96 and POS 0.4578, as the book’s program found.

optsqr(4)
#> ╭── Optimal square searches ────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
#> │   Searches                 1                                              │
#> │   Total effort             4                                              │
#> │   Chance found by the end  0.4578                                         │
#> │                                                                           │
#> │   search  effort  releff  cumeff  factor   side     poc  coverage     pod │
#> │   ------  ------  ------  ------  ------  -----  ------  --------  ------ │
#> │        1       4       4       4   1.021  2.042  0.5940    0.9592  0.7707 │
#> │                                                                           │
#> │   search     pos  cumpos                                                  │
#> │   ------  ------  ------                                                  │
#> │        1  0.4578  0.4578                                                  │
#> │                                                                           │
#> │   Each search covers the square (of side 'side') that gives it the best   │
#> │   chance of success after the searches before it. poc is the chance the   │
#> │   object is in that square, pod the chance of detecting it there, pos     │
#> │   their product and cumpos the running chance it has been found.          │
#> ╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
srchfig("6-3")

srchfig("6-4")

Figure 6-5. By the additive principle, a series of searches each optimal for what the earlier ones left does as well as one optimal search with all the effort: the cumulative probability of success depends on the cumulative effort.

srchfig("6-5")

Figure 6-6. Searching in a series with random efforts between 0.1 and 50 E^2, the optimal factors cluster around the curve, except where a much smaller effort follows a large one and the best use of it is the remaining central peak.

srchfig("6-6")

Your own search

The figures use the book’s numbers; every function takes yours, and each result has a plot() method. srchfig() lists, for each of the 36 figures, the one line that draws it from your own numbers (replace the example inputs; a schematic gives the computation it pictures):

# an HTML table with each line in <code>: in a Markdown table a `$` starts a
# formula and a `|` ends the cell, so both are written as entities
tab <- srchfig()[, c("fig", "caption", "yours")]
esc <- function(x) {
  for (r in list(
    c("&", "&amp;"),
    c("<", "&lt;"),
    c(">", "&gt;"),
    c("$", "&#36;"),
    c("|", "&#124;")
  )) {
    x <- gsub(r[1], r[2], x, fixed = TRUE)
  }
  x
}
tab$caption <- esc(tab$caption)
tab$yours <- sprintf("<code>%s</code>", esc(tab$yours))
knitr::kable(
  tab,
  format = "html",
  escape = FALSE,
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Figure", "Caption", "From your own numbers")
)
Figure Caption From your own numbers

The most used of them, step by step. Say a sensor’s sweep width is 0.8 nautical miles and its detection falls off as the inverse cube of the lateral range. Its lateral range curve, and the picture of what the sweep width means (the objects missed inside it equal those seen outside it, Figure 4-7):

lr <- ltrlrng(seq(-3, 3, by = 0.05), W = 0.8)
plot(lr)

plot(lr, equiv = TRUE)

A sweep width can also come from a field trial: the share of objects detected at each lateral range, measured on both sides of the track. swpwdth() integrates the curve.

d <- c(-3, -2, -1.5, -1, -0.5, -0.25, 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3)
p <- c(0.01, 0.08, 0.2, 0.45, 0.75, 0.9, 0.95, 0.9, 0.75, 0.45, 0.2, 0.08, 0.01)
swpwdth(d, p)
#> [1] 2.03

The probability of detection for the coverage a plan gives (coverage is sweep width times track length over the area), and for parallel sweeps at a track spacing of 1 with a navigation error of 0.1:

pd <- srchpod(seq(0, 3, by = 0.1), model = "invcube")
plot(pd)

pswppod(W = 0.8, S = 1, navsd = 0.1)
#> [1] 0.6806056

After a search of three areas that found nothing, the chance the object is in each area is updated by what each search could have detected:

srchscs(poc = c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2), pod = c(0.8, 0.5, 0))
#> ╭── Probability of success ────────────────────────────────────────────╮
#> │   Areas        3                                                     │
#> │   Searches     1                                                     │
#> │   Overall POS  0.55                                                  │
#> │                                                                      │
#> │   area     poc  cumpod  posarea  pocupd                              │
#> │   ----  ------  ------  -------  ------                              │
#> │      1  0.5000  0.8000   0.4000  0.2222                              │
#> │      2  0.3000  0.5000   0.1500  0.3333                              │
#> │      3  0.2000  0.0000   0.0000  0.4444                              │
#> │                                                                      │
#> │   POS 0.55 after 1 search                                            │
#> │   poc: chance the object is in the area; cumpod: chance the searches │
#> │   detect it there; pocupd: the poc after the searches found nothing. │
#> ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

Your own search, step by step

The same functions plan a real search from your own numbers, one call per step. Use one distance unit throughout (kilometres here; nautical miles at sea): the grid, the positions, the sweep width and the track length are all in it, and areas in its square.

1. The search area and its grid. A hiker is overdue; the last known position (LKP) is 2 km east and 3 km north of the base. Lay a grid of cells over the area you could search: here 12 km by 12 km in half-kilometre cells. xedg and yedg are the cell edges, west to east and south to north; cells need not be equal.

xe <- seq(-4, 8, by = 0.5)
ye <- seq(-3, 9, by = 0.5)

2. The probability map. datumpmap() puts the chance the hiker is in each cell on the grid. For a point datum give the LKP as center and the position error as sigma, one standard deviation (about 1.5 km, from the time and terrain since the LKP). A route between two points is datum = "line" or "corridor" with end, a region known only by its bounds datum = "area", and a map of your own (cell shares from the planners’ scenarios, say) is datum = "general" with wts, one row per y cell and one column per x cell.

m <- datumpmap(xe, ye, center = c(2, 3), sigma = 1.5)
m
#> ╭── Datum probability map (point datum) ──────────────────────────────────╮
#> │   Datum   point                                                         │
#> │   Centre  2, 3                                                          │
#> │   Sigma   1.5                                                           │
#> │   Grid    24 x 24 cells (x by y)                                        │
#> │                                                                         │
#> │   The most likely cells                                                 │
#> │       x      y      poc                                                 │
#> │   -----  -----  -------                                                 │
#> │   1.750  2.750  0.01705                                                 │
#> │   1.750  3.250  0.01705                                                 │
#> │   2.250  2.750  0.01705                                                 │
#> │   2.250  3.250  0.01705                                                 │
#> │   1.250  2.750  0.01527                                                 │
#> │                                                                         │
#> │   24 x 24 cells (x by y); 0.0% of the probability lies outside the grid │
#> ╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
plot(m)

Two scenarios weighted by the planners (70% on the LKP, 30% that the hiker took the trail to the north-east) are mixed cell by cell, and the mixture is a general datum (its weights are scaled to sum to 1 over the grid):

trail <- datumpmap(xe, ye, "corridor", c(2, 3), sigma = 0.5, end = c(2, 8))
mix <- datumpmap(xe, ye, "general", wts = 0.7 * m$poc + 0.3 * trail$poc)
plot(mix)

3. The sweep width and the detection model. The sweep width W comes from a published table for the sensor, the object and the conditions, or from a field trial of your own with swpwdth() (above). The detection model says how detection falls off with distance: "invcube" for good conditions and evenly spaced tracks, "random" for poor conditions or uneven tracks (the conservative choice), "definite" for a sensor that sees everything within W / 2. Here the ground teams’ sweep width is 0.6 km.

4. Effort, and the probability of detection. The effort is the track length walked in each cell. Say today’s teams walked 2 km of track in each of the four cells round the LKP. srchpod() with W, effort and area turns that into the coverage and the POD of each cell; area = m takes the map’s cell areas, and effort is laid out like the map (one row per y cell):

walked <- matrix(0, nrow(m$poc), ncol(m$poc))
walked[12:13, 12:13] <- 2
pd <- srchpod(W = 0.6, effort = walked, area = m, model = "random")
range(pd)
#> [1] 0.0000000 0.9917703

5. The probability of success, and the map after a search that found nothing. srchscs() takes the map and the PODs: pos is the chance today’s search found the hiker, and map the probability map updated by what was searched (cells searched hard become less likely, the rest more likely):

day1 <- srchscs(m, pd)
day1
#> ╭── Probability of success ────────────────────────────────────────────╮

#> │                                                                      │
#> │   The 20 most likely of 576 cells.                                   │
#> ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
plot(day1$map)

6. Plan the next search. opteffort() spreads tomorrow’s 40 km of track over the updated map to make the chance of finding the hiker as large as possible (Stone 1975), under random search detection. Its result goes straight back into srchscs() for the day after:

day2 <- opteffort(day1$map, W = 0.6, effort = 40)
day2

#> [1] 0.546653

7. Plot. Every result has a plot() method: the allocation as a map of the effort in each cell, the map as an image, a surface or its cells with their percentages.

plot(day2)

plot(day1$map, view = "both")

For a single point datum with no grid, optcrcsrch() gives Koopman’s optimal circle directly, and optsqr() the optimal square, search after search:

optcrcsrch(sigma = 1.5, W = 0.6, effort = 40)
#> ╭── Optimal search of a circular normal datum ────────────────────────╮
#> │   sigma    1.5                                                      │
#> │   W        0.6                                                      │
#> │   effort   40                                                       │
#> │   radius   2.88                                                     │
#> │   pos      0.5497                                                   │
#> │   cntrdns  3.071                                                    │
#> │                                                                     │
#> │   Spread the effort evenly over a circle of radius 2.88: the chance │
#> │   of finding the object is then 55.0%.                              │
#> │                                                                     │
#> │   cntrdns: the coverage at the centre of the circle.                │
#> ╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
optsqr(c(40, 40) * 0.6, E = 1.1774 * 1.5)
#> ╭── Optimal square searches ────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
#> │   Searches                 2                                              │
#> │   Total effort             48                                             │
#> │   Chance found by the end  0.8047                                         │
#> │                                                                           │
#> │   search  effort  releff  cumeff  factor   side     poc  coverage     pod │
#> │   ------  ------  ------  ------  ------  -----  ------  --------  ------ │
#> │        1      24   7.695    7.69   1.270  4.485  0.7484    1.1929  0.8651 │
#> │        2      24   7.695   15.39   1.696  5.991  0.7460    0.6686  0.5980 │
#> │                                                                           │
#> │   search     pos  cumpos                                                  │
#> │   ------  ------  ------                                                  │
#> │        1  0.6475  0.6475                                                  │
#> │        2  0.4461  0.8047                                                  │
#> │                                                                           │
#> │   Each search covers the square (of side 'side') that gives it the best   │
#> │   chance of success after the searches before it. poc is the chance the   │
#> │   object is in that square, pod the chance of detecting it there, pos     │
#> │   their product and cumpos the running chance it has been found.          │
#> ╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

References

Frost, J. R. (1996). The Theory of Search: A Simplified Explanation. Soza and Company and U.S. Coast Guard Office of Search and Rescue. Chapters 3-6 and their figures.

Koopman, B. O. (1946). Search and Screening. OEG Report 56, Office of the Chief of Naval Operations.

Koopman, B. O. (1956-1957). The theory of search, parts I-III. Operations Research 4(3), 324-346; 4(5), 503-531; 5(5), 613-626.

Stone, L. D. (1975). Theory of Optimal Search. Academic Press.
